title: Quietism and Activism - Difficult and Easy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights the importance of embracing paradox and ambiguity, rather than trying to categorize experiences as "easy" or "difficult." This is reflected in the story of Leman Pong, who sat with his family studying sutras but ultimately realized that neither perspective was fully accurate - we simply need to show up and be present. By letting go of our need for labels and judgments, we can cultivate a sense of openness, kindness, and curiosity that supports both quietism and activism, and inspires us to live more mindfully and authentically.

sentences.text: Good afternoon, everybody.
Thanks for being here.
Thanks for coming if you're just arriving from somewhere.
*Leman Pong was sitting in his thatched cottage one day with his family studying the sutras.
"Difficult, difficult, difficult," he suddenly exclaimed.
"Like trying to store ten bushels of sesame seed in the top of a tree."
"Easy, easy, easy," his wife, Laywoman Pong, answered.
"It's like touching your feet to the floor when you get out of bed."
"Neither difficult nor easy," said their daughter, Ningzhao.
"It's like the teachings of the ancestors shining on the hundred grass tips."*
You might not believe me, but I don't think I've ever mentioned Leman Pong in a Dharma talk, and I was already planning to before I knew Norman was going to do that.
That's kind of weird.
Difficult, difficult, difficult, or is it easy, easy, easy, or neither difficult nor easy?
What a beautiful image: the teachings of the ancestors shining on the hundred grass tips.
Have you ever on a sunny morning really looked at the dew on the grass tips?
I think the diamond industry would collapse if we really looked carefully at dew drops, don't you think?
They're just as beautiful, maybe more.
A few more thoughts about Leman Pong.
The book called The Recording Sayings of Leman Pong was amongst the early English-language literature on Zen, published I think in 1971.
It was co-written by a really interesting person, Ruth Fuller Suzuki, a pioneering Western woman involved in Japanese Zen.
The book says the sayings of Leman Pong, but actually a lot of them are stories about the Pong family, the whole family.
These are family stories, and each of the three members of this family may be showing us a different facet of our life.
We are all three of them, aren't we?
Leman Pong: so difficult.
Laywoman Pong: nothing, it's easy.
And then maybe somewhere, when we listen carefully, their daughter, not caught in that duality of easy and difficult.

And this story makes me think about the journey of our Shuso: her preparation and her work during the practice period, which she shared with us so beautifully through her talks and her Dharma of anger class and just by hanging around.
Being Shuso is definitely difficult, difficult, difficult, right?
A previous version of Connie would have answered differently.
It does sound difficult, though, to our mind that divides things into difficult and easy.
All the stuff you have to do.
Show up with your peers in a whole new way, in a new role.
There's no hiding as the Shuso.
You take the teacher's seat for the duration of the practice period, share the teacher's seat.
You're asked to open your heart and open your mouth and teach in the community.
And this can be intimidating.
But also, true enough, it's easy, easy, easy.
The word Shuso actually means head seat, chief seat, like these kinds of seats.
So the actual job is done completely with your butt, not your head.
You have to sit there.
Your job is to sit there, to hold that seat, to take that seat, to hold that space.
You get to have tea with the wondrous members of the community and get to know them a little better.
What a delight.
You realize once you start teaching the classes that really your job is to listen more than to speak, and to include and honor and support the wisdom all around you.
And Connie did that beautifully in her class, giving lots of room for us to talk to each other, inviting different sangha members to share a few words in each class.
There's nothing to it.
You just ride the waves and coordinate.
Connie's been in close contact with me after each of those six or seven classes, which I've appreciated very much.
And finally, this last Wednesday night, after the last of her classes, in which Connie said almost nothing, she opened and had each of us share a little bit of what we've learned about anger.
It was fascinating.
Every one of us seems to have a different relationship to anger or a different sense of anger.
Realizing anger is just a five-letter word, or a concept for something deep in our gut, deep in our heart.
And at the end, Connie just said a little bit.
Afterwards, she shared with me that she had all this other stuff prepared that she was going to say, but realized it was not needed.
It's enough.
And then she said to me, "Well, the class is done."
Easy.
A sense of ease.
Nothing to worry about.
And she's giving her first formal Dharma talk during sesshin, which is kind of a thing.
Done.
In a way, this question of easy and difficult is exactly the conversation Connie and I have been having for fifteen or sixteen years, something like that.
One of us taking one position or the other.
Things around here seem really difficult.
They seem really easy.
Me often tending to express the easy side: don't worry about it, no biggie.
And we've gotten into some tangles at times about this.
Maybe you've gotten into tangles with people in the same way.
One of you taking one position, "This is going to be really difficult," the other taking the other position, "What are you so worried about?
Come on, relax."
Neither of which helps the other, right?
At all.
And maybe now both Connie and I can realize, and we can all realize together with each other, that either position is missing the mark.
Either position is a kind of dividing and simplifying things in a way that's not going to help us or the world.
"Neither difficult nor easy," said Peng Ling Zhao.
Teaching's shining through, everywhere.
The hundred grass tips means everywhere.
Everywhere in the universe, everywhere you can imagine, everywhere you can see or not see is shining through.
Just like the colors in cedar tree bark.
Just like the glistening eyes of a deer.
Just like the moist eyes of another human being when we actually look and actually receive each other.
We don't have to figure out what's easy or difficult anymore.
But we do, it seems like, have to really show up, even if we don't know what to do or how to do it.
We can make tons of plans or no plans.
It's unclear to me which is better at this point.
And showing up is not so easy, but it's also not so difficult.
It's showing up.
I want to make a little aside to talk about Ruth Fuller Suzuki, because she lived an unbelievable life, and just to honor another pioneering Zen woman as we honor Connie this weekend.
I was going to read you a whole section of this book.
I think now I'll just share a little bit about her.
There's a recent book out about her called Zen Odyssey.
It's not the best book ever written, but it's a wonderful offering nonetheless.
These authors spent five or six years talking to her relations and digging into the history, talking to everybody, anybody who remembered anything from any of the characters involved.
Ruth Fuller Suzuki was born Ruth Fuller in 1892 in Chicago to a wealthy, educated family.
So she had indeed some class advantages and race advantages: white woman.
But she was a woman growing up at the turn of the century, and she was duly married off to a banker many years her senior, who was in poor health.
He died I think when she was about 40.

And somehow in her childhood, I don't remember how, and it says in great detail in the book so we could look, she got interested in Eastern philosophy, just kind of on her own, as a teenager or in her young twenties maybe, reading all about this stuff.
And then she and her wealthy husband did some world tours, and on one of them she convinced him that they needed to go to Japan.
He wasn't interested in it.
They went to Japan, and she somehow connected with the famous D.T.
Suzuki, who was part of every story of Zen in the West somehow.
I don't know how he got around that much.
And she didn't want to just learn philosophy or study with D.T.
Suzuki, who a little bit later ended up at Columbia in New York.
She really wanted to practice.

And in the 1930s, I don't have it down here, maybe '36 or '37, somehow she finagled to spend three months living in a house next to a temple, a house owned by the temple priest, doing zazen full time.
There's a fabulous story in the book about this.
Mostly just on her own, getting up, doing solo sesshin for a couple of months, and having a big awakening experience.
And eventually she went on to marry Sokeyan Suzuki, who was a Japanese pioneer in New York, and he soon died after that.
She ended up in Japan in 1958, becoming the first foreigner to become ordained in the Rinzai Zen tradition.
Not the first female foreigner.
The first foreigner, period.
And the only Westerner, and the only woman to date, to be given priesthood, given an abbessy of a temple in the Rinzai Zen tradition.
She was given the abbessy of a sub-temple at Daitokuji, which [unclear: "Artenza"] was just talking about.
And she was part of why Gary Snyder ended up there.
She used her resources to start a translation and study bureau and invited young scholars.
Somehow Gary Snyder and others that we've heard had ended up there.
So I just wanted to give a little shout-out to Ruth Fuller Suzuki.
She was also apparently a very domineering person and kind of difficult to be around, like most people who get stuff done.
Did I say something?

There were some details about when she first got involved in the Buddhist Society of America, which became the First Zen Institute of America, the organization that grew up around this Japanese priest in New York, in his apartment, Sokayan.
And they managed to talk to relatives of survivors, who said, "Oh yeah, she drove everybody crazy."
She bowled in there, wanted to be in charge of all the committees.
And she also had all the money.
It's not like any of us are perfect, but we make our contribution, right?

And somehow Ruth Fuller Suzuki, like so many other of these pioneers (we talked about Jiyu-Kennett a couple of years ago, same thing), didn't believe whatever story of difficult, difficult, difficult she would have been taught deeply, right, about doing what she did, helping to bring Zen to the West in that way.
Which all brings us, I think somehow, to the question of activism, which both Connie and Norman brought up so powerfully.
I really appreciated their talks, and I also appreciated being a bit challenged by their talks.
Did you feel a little challenged by those talks?
We should feel a little challenged, shouldn't we?
If our whole thing here was just to celebrate what great buddies we are and how nice it is to be in this beautiful place, maybe that wouldn't be quite enough.
And the problems in the world do seem difficult, difficult, difficult, don't they?
So I was thinking about activism and quietism.
Quietism kind of has a bad rap, and activism is great.
We all like activism.
So I don't know if you are up to date on this, and I might be a little out of date.
But did you know that the student activists at Marjorie Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, decided to throw up a GoFundMe to support their efforts?
Do you know about this?
I read this in a major news outlet, so I think it's actually true.
But the part I'm about to say is, being teenagers who have a certain orientation towards what should happen, they put a one-million-dollar goal in their GoFundMe campaign to support their activism.
You can imagine their parents, in the wake of this tragedy, wanting to be supportive but kind of resisting the urge to say, "No, don't put that.
How about 10,000?"
They didn't.
They put one million dollars.
The first million was raised by 1,400 individuals.
The next half million was given by George Clooney.
Then George Clooney calls up all his buddies, and they're at about three and a half million dollars now.
So somehow the world is seeing such tremendous hope and possibility in these young people who just survived a horror like that.
That's pretty wonderful and exciting.

On Monday after the Valentine's Day shooting, some students at Sehome High School, and then I think they connected with a few friends at Bellingham High and Squalicum High, the three high schools of Bellingham, started communicating with each other on whichever Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook Messenger they use.
There's a million of them you've never heard of.
Email's way too old school for these guys.
Anyway, they started talking about, well, maybe we should rally.
Maybe we should gather.
That was Monday after school.

On Wednesday, two thousand of them converged on City Hall and had a student-organized rally, for which they successfully got permits from the police, permission of the city authorities, and negotiated the support of the school administration.

As a parent, I get the emails from the school principal and the school superintendent saying, "Well, of course we would like our children to be in school, but we want you to know, dear parents, that we support the efforts of our students."
They gave us a little background about how they organized this and the things they just told you.

And they also wisely said, "We don't want any student to feel pressured, and we want each student to make a choice, and it's up to you as the parent or guardian to decide whether to excuse the absence, but we support this effort."
Apparently some districts in other places are suspending and punishing children for walking out in protest like that.
So I went last Wednesday at noon.
Speakers were eloquent, with a few little teenage things in there.
You're still 16, 17, 18.
The first one was a young woman talking about living with constant suicidal thoughts since she was ten years old, until finally someone identified that there's a mental health issue here.
She started treatment with a really good psychologist, a little medication, lots of therapy.
She said, yeah, it's still hard to be in my head sometimes, but I'm living a good life now.
And I want you to know that if I had access to a gun when I was 13 or 14, I don't think I'd be here.
And there was lots of other discussion about the political situation and the failings of their olders and not so betters.
Very eloquent, very powerful.
I stood there just thinking, wow, I'm bearing witness to a historic moment.
These young people, maybe they'll save us.
Maybe they'll save us after all.
There are some more young people out there.
But then on the walk home, I also started to think, well, am I just abdicating my responsibility?
Why was I just watching on the fringes?
Difficult, easy, neither.
I got all fired up though.
We have a little bit of money, so I wanted to send Walker and his buddies to D.C. if they wanted to be part of the next protest.
But Walker's like, yeah.
But he did walk out with his friends.
They participated in the rally.
Then they got pizza.
It's so hopeful and so exciting.

And then I watched a little bit of the news about the kids in Florida going down to the Florida state legislature and speaking their minds, and receiving a complex mix of support and resistance and rejection from the adults they were talking to.
And then I got this email from the Southern Poverty Law Center, pointing out a huge blind spot that I had not even thought of.
What color are all these children talking to these legislatures, raising all this money with George Clooney, getting all this media attention and accolades?
I also heard a little radio piece interviewing a few of the kids involved, just talking about how flooded they are with messages of support, letters and emails, on all channels.
Flooded.
It's overwhelming to them.
Of course, meanwhile, they're suffering from the stress of what they witnessed and the friends they lost.
So here's what the Southern Poverty Law Center points out.
*This week began with the sixth anniversary of Trayvon Martin's death.
And it will end with a march commemorating the 53rd anniversary of Bloody Sunday, the day voting rights activists were beaten by lawmen in Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge.
By any measure, it's a week steeped in not only the history of racial inequality in America, but also in our rich history of activism.

And nowhere is it more evident than at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, where students have riveted the country with their pleas for gun reform after the horrific Valentine's Day that left 17 students and teachers dead.
The students have relentlessly told their story, organized marches and pressured politicians.
Their work, quote, converting grief into power, as Niti Upadhyayi detailed for the New York Times, is part of a powerful legacy of American youth activism.
In 1960, for example, teenagers led the civil rights movement when they conducted sit-ins at a Woolworth's lunch counter.

A year later, young people endured brutal beatings on the Freedom Rides aimed at desegregating bus stations in the Deep South, and two years after that, children as young as six braved police dogs and fire hoses in the 1963 Children's Crusade to end racial segregation in Birmingham, Alabama.*
*Many in these last two weeks have hailed students in Parkland, Florida as the descendants of these courageous civil rights activists.
But they are not the only, or even the first, teens working in the 21st century to end gun violence.

In the wake of Trayvon Martin's death at the hands of a security guard in 2012, young people mobilized under the name Black Lives Matter to demand reforms very similar to those now articulated by the students in Parkland.
These students did not receive the same support or recognition that the nation has given Parkland students in these last two weeks.
The way people are responding to predominantly white communities is notable.
"Whose movement is more valuable to support?" asked Dante Berry, co-founder of the racial justice group Million Hoodies.
Writing for Teen Vogue, Lincoln Anthony Blades was more direct.
"Black youth who've been passionately advocating for gun control measures have been demonized, obfuscated, and overlooked.
And black young people are disproportionately affected by gun violence.
And for years they've been organizing.
Organizing anti-violence rallies, meeting with presidential candidates, proposing policy ideas, and holding weeks-long sit-ins.
And they too have taken on the NRA."*
*Parkland students themselves have credited Black Lives Matter for serving as a model for how to demand gun reform.
"Much of what I've done and wanted to do was inspired by Black Lives Matter," said one of the students.
"We're protesting the exact same way and being called heroes.
Just because the majority of us are white.
America needs to do better in so many ways."
The fact that we have not given Black Lives Matter the same support we have given the students in Parkland should give us pause.* And they conclude their email saying:
*In the wake of unimaginable tragedy, we should celebrate Parkland students' success in calling for such urgently needed reform.
At the same time we have to own up to the nation's blind spot when it comes to who gets empathy in America, and ask the question of whether it's race that makes all the difference.*
So struck by that.
You know, the thing about blind spots is you don't see them until you see them, right?
It seems so obvious, picturing those white, articulate, well-dressed young men and women at the Florida legislature last week.
I was trying to think about how our practice, how the quietism side of this, is important and really matters.
And I've thought about this a lot since the last presidential election.

I think what keeps coming back to me as most important, and it's probably the most difficult for us to talk about or share with anybody, is this teaching from Laman Pong and his family: the way the mind so easily divides things up into this or that, right?
And the whole nation is just awash in us and them, this and that, black and white, right and wrong, liberal, conservative, and so on and so forth.
We're not liberal or conservative, are we?
Neither liberal nor conservative, liberal and conservative, just people.

And somehow, who knows how exactly, intensive training in zazen and the teachings that have been brought and given and offered to us with such generosity help us to develop a heart that can hold these opposites without needing to cling to one side or the other so fiercely.
Somehow it cultivates a kind of openness, a kindness that can still exist in the face of horror and strife and difficulty.
Maybe the only way we can share that is by modeling it in our lives.
I don't know.
It's the first thing I thought of: this kind of holding opposites.
It's working with the dualities of the mind and little by little freeing ourselves from that narrowness of division.

And we do this experientially in this kind of contrived situation, wearing our funny outfits, where we decide some things are really important, like who gets to give the Dharma talk, or who gets to be Shuso, or which way you should turn when you stand up for K'in Hin, or how you should serve the food.
On purpose, we make these unimportant things very, very important to study our crazy minds.
We get upset with each other.
We get so delighted with each other.
The whole drama of humanity unfolds within this one room, doesn't it, and inside our own minds.
It's a serious business.
So this is a kind of training for the world, isn't it?
So I thought of holding opposites, and I also thought of being able to hold suffering without turning away from it, which we're practicing in just a hands-on, embodied way, right?

Just by sitting still for half an hour at a time through the waves of the mind and the pain in the body, practicing a kind of non-reactivity and a kind of being with, or holding, or whatever language you use, practicing not something that's beyond language.
How can we just be with suffering in a way that's creative and open, non-reactive and felt, really felt, not turning away?
And then I think of a song.
If you know this, feel free to join me.
For some reason, I've had Cat Stevens on my mind a lot.
He reemerged in the public music scene, did you know that, a couple of years ago, apparently?
I didn't catch it when he first came back.
He went into hiding for decades, and now he's singing his original catalog.
Yeah, who knew?
This came out in 1971, the same time as Ruth Fuller Suzuki's book and Layman Pong.
So it all goes together.
*Trouble, oh trouble, set me free.
I have seen your face and it's too much, too much for me.
Trouble, oh trouble, can't you see?
You're eating my heart away and there's nothing much left of me.
I've drunk your wine.
You have made your world mine.
So won't you be fair?
So won't you be fair?
I don't want no more of you.
So won't you be kind to me?
Just let me go where I'll have to go there.
Trouble, oh trouble, move away.
I have seen your face and it's too much for me today.*
So our practice, I think, helps us to be with the trouble.
And that's important.
How much of the suffering and strife in the world is sideways emanations of a heart destroyed by trouble, not able to hold the suffering of being a person?
And as Norman mentioned, it's embarrassing to be in a way so privileged, but still there's suffering.
And maybe in the little way we can, we can share a practice of being with, starting wherever we start.
And then there are so many practical ways our practice helps that are easier to talk about with people and demonstrate and share.
One is just slowing down, for goodness' sake, right?
We need this odd structure that we've inherited slash created to just get us to stop.
We need the group effect.
All of us would be embarrassed if we ran out of here and got on our phones.
So we stay through our busyness and our craziness, and that flows out into our lives.
I just went on a little walk today, and I was coming up towards the stoplight, or the stop sign, and the pedestrian signal had the countdown thing.
I was about a quarter of the block away and it was on four or five, right?
I could have gone for it.
Which is this deep habit, right?
This deep habit that's so infectious that we share.
We're good at sharing hurry.
We hurry with each other.
Maybe we can practice sharing non-hurry with each other.

So I actually slowed down, and I could actually somehow, after a day and a half of sitting here, remember at At least once there's a pleasure in just standing here quietly at the corner, breathing and feeling the sun.
A beautiful day.
I was not in a hurry.
That made me think of another snippet from the early 70s.
This is an early, early 70s talk, I guess.
I was alive then.
I was pretty young.
In 1972, some psychologist from Princeton published a famous psychological study that's much cited even to this day.

I'm always a little nervous about citing research, because as an outsider I don't know which research is really good, but I've heard this cited by people that I know to be good researchers, so I'll assume it's good.
This is called the Good Samaritan study.
Have you heard of this study?
I've quoted it before, but it's worth remembering.
I love these clever studies where they trick people to find out how we actually act, if we're not just responding to what we think someone else wants us to do.
What we really do when nobody's looking, kind of.
They took a bunch of seminarians at Princeton, and they told them, great news, we have an extra special super seminar for you on writing outstanding seminars, or sermons, writing good sermons.
It's optional, you can sign up for it.
Little did the young seminarians know that they were signing up for a psychology study.
They gave them some standard coaching on how to write a good sermon, and half of them were invited to write a sermon on the story of the Good Samaritan.
The other half were invited to write a sermon on job opportunities in the pastoral world or something like that, a practical talk for seminarians.
The researchers were curious to see if reflecting on the story of the Good Samaritan, reflecting on good moral values, reflecting on ethics, would affect behavior.
That was one variable.
The other variable was hurry.
They divided things into six quadrants.
There was the Good Samaritan talk and the job talk, and then there were three hurry conditions.
For the high hurry kids, somebody sidles up to them as they're just barely finishing writing their talk and says, really sorry, we kind of blew the timing.
You're late.
You've got to deliver this talk.
It's across campus.
You really better go.
The low hurry kids were told, when you finish up, you've got some time, but you probably should get down there.
And then they had some message for the medium hurry condition.

Somehow, I don't know how they do all this, they organized it so that the seminarians ended up walking alone down the campus pathways, and they had a Confederate there walking along who suddenly falls down and moans in pain in front of the seminarian.
And the data is: what does the seminarian do?
Does he or she stop and help?
Do they keep going?
Do they remember later and try to call somebody?
What do they do?
Well, we'll start with the depressing news.
Only 10% of the high hurry seminarians stopped.
I know.
There was a small effect from whether they were giving their talk about the story of the Good Samaritan, but it was not statistically significant.
The other end of the spectrum, still a little disappointing: 63% of the low hurry seminarians stopped.
The data summary I saw didn't say how many of the others later said, "I saw somebody back there, but I had to get to my talk."
So I don't know.
But it is true, isn't it, in our experience?
When we're stressed out, when we're in a rush, we have too much to do, we're not so available, are we?
Not too available to the world.
I'm not too available to help.
So this is so simple, but yeah.
We're training deeply in a non-hurry condition here.
Maybe we all keep nurturing that and don't let it just fade away a few days from now.
Can we devote ourselves to presence, to openness?
So those are the four things I thought of.
There's a lot more.
It's not a definitive list, the ways that quietism might support activism.
I actually know there's one more.
I only mentioned three.
So we'll do one more.
I'll close with one more.
I thought of holding opposites, being able to not divide things up so much, being able to hold suffering, and devoting ourselves to slowing down.
And the last one is to increase our curiosity about perception, to recognize through our time on the cushion, our interactions with each other, our interactions with our teachers, that the world...
Thank you very much.
You're a good mind reader.
Good training.
That the world we think is out there is actually a world that we are perceiving and manufacturing.
We're taking in little bits of data through our senses, with thoughts bubbling up, and we're constructing a world.
It's not always exactly the same world that everyone else is in.
Maybe never.
So I've got a cute little story on perception to close my talk, which is also a Connie reference.
I read this little story before in a Dharma talk on perception.
That was Connie's favorite talk because it was my funniest ever talk.
So here's the story, a little story called "Museum."
It's a prose piece written by a poet, so it's very efficient prose.
The writing geeks in the audience can appreciate that as it unfolds.
It's about three and a half, three pages maybe.
I have the complete little story here, just to plant that seed of curiosity about whether what we're perceiving is really the world.
We're so upset about the world sometimes, but is it really the world?
This is Naomi Shihab Nye, Palestinian American poet, wonderful person, speaking.
*I was 17.
My family had just moved to San Antonio.
A local magazine featured an alluring article about a museum called the McNay, an old mansion once the home of an eccentric, many times married watercolorist named Marion Coogler McNay.
She had deeded it to the community to become a museum upon her death.
I asked my friend Sally, who drove a cute little convertible and had just moved to Texas the year before we did, if she wanted to go there.
Sally said, sure.
She was a good friend that way.
We had made up a few words in our own language and we could dissolve into laughter just by saying our words.
Our mothers thought we were a bit odd.*
*And so on a bright, sunny Saturday afternoon, we drove over to Broadway.
Sally asked, "Do you have the address of this place?"
"No," I said, "but just drive slowly.
I'll recognize it.
There was a picture in the magazine."
I peered in both directions and pointed, saying, "There it is.
Pull in."
The parking lot under some palm trees was pretty empty.
We entered excited.
The museum was free.
Right away, the spirit of the arched doorways, carved window frames and elegant artwork overtook us.
Sally went left.
I went right.
A group of people seated in some chairs in the lobby stopped talking and stared at us.
"May I help you?" a man said.
"No," I said, "we're fine.
I don't like to talk to people in museums.
Tours and docents get on my nerves."
What if they talked a long time about paintings that you weren't interested in?
I took a deep breath and moved on to another painting.
Fireworks over a patio in Mexico, maybe?*
*There weren't very good tags in this museum.
In fact, there weren't any.
I stood back and gazed.
Sally had gone upstairs.
The people in the lobby had stopped chatting.
They seemed very nosy, keeping their eyes on me with irritating curiosity.
What was their problem?
I turned down a hallway.
Bougainvillea and azalea pressed up right against the windows.
Maybe we should have brought a picnic.
Was that a Moorish courtyard?
I saw some nice sculptures in another room and a small couch.
This would be a great place for reading.
Above the couch hung a radiant print by Paul Klee, my favorite artist, blues and pinks merging softly in his own wonderful way.
I stepped closer.
Suddenly I became aware of a man from the lobby standing behind me in the doorway.
"Where do you think you are?" he asked.
I turned sharply.
"The McNay Art Museum."
He smiled then and shook his head.
"Sorry to tell you, the McNay is three blocks over on New Brunfell Street.
Take a right when you go out of our driveway, then another right."
"What is this place?"
I asked, still confused.
He said, "Well, we thought it was our home."*
*My heart jolted.
I raced past him to the bottom of the staircase and called out, "Sally, come down immediately.
Urgent."
I remember being tempted to shout something in our private language, but we didn't have a word for this.
Sally came to the top of the stairs smiling happily and said, "You have to come up here.
There's really good stuff.
And there's old beds."
"No, Sally, no," I said, as if she were a dog or a baby.
"Get down here.
Speed it up.
Emergency."
Sally stepped elegantly down the stairs as if in a museum trance, looking puzzled.
I just couldn't tell her out loud in front of these people what we had done.
I actually pushed her towards the front door, waving my hands at the family in the chairs, saying, "Sorry, oh my God, please forgive us.
You have a really nice place.
Bye."*
That's like one word.
*Sally stared at me in the parking lot.
When I told her, she covered her mouth and doubled over with laughter, shaking.
We were still in their yard.
I imagined them inside looking out the windows at us.
She couldn't believe how long they'd let us look around without saying anything.
"That was really friendly of them," she said.
"Get in the car," I said.
The real McNay was fabulous.
Splendid.
But we felt a little nervous the whole time.
Van Gogh, Picasso, Tamayo.
This time there were tags.
This time we stayed together in case something else happened.
And we never told anyone.*
*Thirty years later, a nice looking woman approached me in a public place.
"Excuse me," she said.
"I need to ask you a strange question.
Did you ever, by any chance, enter a residence long ago thinking it was the McNay Museum?"
Thirty years later, my cheeks still burned.
"Yes," I said.
"But how do you know?
I never told anyone."
"That was my home," she said.
"I was a teenager sitting with my family, talking in the living room.
Before you came over, I never realized what a beautiful place I lived in.
I never felt lucky before.
You thought it was a museum.
My feelings changed about my parents after that too.
They had [unclear: "a really good case"].
They had good taste.
They were really good to me.
I realized that in that day.
And I've always wanted to thank you."*
So not always, but halfway, sometimes our perceptual mess-ups are beneficial to people too.
We'll get to say lots of gratitude things tomorrow, but it's time to stop.
I just want to say thank you to everybody, to Connie and Norman and everybody in the Sangha, everybody who has been here a long time or a little time.
And just to express this hope that what we're doing is not just about having a quietism club.
Something bigger.
And it's difficult and it's easy and it's neither.
Maybe some of us will continue the excellent work we're already doing out in the world.
Maybe some of us will be inspired to do more.
Maybe some of us will just focus on keeping places like this, taking care of places of peace and renewal, whatever this is called.
Because it all, I think, matters in ways that probably we can't totally understand.
Maybe sometime 30 years from now somebody will say, "Did you ever live in Bellingham?"
Or wherever you live.
So let's just do our best to do whatever that is for each of us.
Thank you.
